html:
The Battle of Dyrrhachium was fought on 10 July 48 BCE near Dyrrhachium, today's Durrës in Albania. Pompey broke through the siege lines of Julius Caesar and forced him to retreat. It was Caesar's worst setback in the civil war.

In Caesar's civil war, Pompey had left Italy and built up a large army in Greece, supplied by sea through Dyrrhachium. Caesar crossed the Adriatic in winter with fewer men and little food. He could not take the port, so he dug a ring of forts and ditches about 25 kilometres long to shut Pompey's larger army against the coast. Pompey built his own line inside it. Then two Gallic deserters told Pompey where Caesar's line was weak, at its southern end by the sea. Pompey attacked there and broke through. A counterattack by Caesar ended in panic, and he lost about 1,000 men.

Pompey did not follow up. Caesar said the enemy would have won that day if they had had a commander who knew how to win. He marched into Thessaly, Pompey followed, and a month later Caesar beat him at Pharsalus. A different battle was fought at the same city in 1081.
